concept: Given a string, determine whether it is a palindrome. Consider only alphanumeric characters and ignore letter casing. Return true if it is a palindrome, false otherwise.

solutions.label: Reverse and Compare
solutions.summary: Filter the string to keep only alphanumeric characters, convert to lowercase, reverse it, and compare with the original filtered string.

solutions.label: Two Pointer In-Place
solutions.summary: Use two pointers from both ends, skip non-alphanumeric characters, and compare characters moving inward.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Here is today's problem. You are given a string that may contain letters, digits, spaces, and punctuation. Your task is to determine if it is a palindrome. However, you should only consider alphanumeric characters and ignore letter casing.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: So I need to check if the string reads the same forwards and backwards, but I should skip over spaces and punctuation and treat uppercase and lowercase as equal. Is that correct?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Exactly. For example, the string 'A man, a plan, a canal: Panama' is a valid palindrome because after removing non-alphanumeric characters and lowering the case, it becomes 'amanaplanacanalpanama', which reads the same in both directions.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: What about edge cases? Should an empty string be considered a palindrome? And will the input always be a valid string?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Yes, an empty string counts as a palindrome. The input is always a valid string and can have a length up to two hundred thousand characters.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Understood. So given a string, I filter it to alphanumeric characters only, convert to lowercase, and check if it is a palindrome. I should return true or false. Let me think about approaches.

sections.title: Reverse and Compare
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    A["Input: 'A man, a plan, a canal: Panama'"] --> B["Filter and lowercase"]
    B --> C["filtered = 'amanaplanacanalpanama'"]
    C --> D["Reverse the filtered string"]
    D --> E["reversed = 'amanaplanacanalpanama'"]
    E --> F{"filtered equals reversed?"}
    F -->|Yes| G["Return true"]
    style A fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style C fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style E fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style G fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: My first approach is straightforward. I will iterate through the string, keep only alphanumeric characters, and convert each to lowercase. This gives me a cleaned string. Then I reverse that cleaned string and compare it with the original cleaned version.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Can you walk through the example?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Sure. For 'A man, a plan, a canal: Panama', after filtering I get 'amanaplanacanalpanama'. Reversing it gives me the same string 'amanaplanacanalpanama'. Since they match, I return true.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: What is the time and space complexity?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The time complexity is O of n because I scan the string once to filter and once to reverse. The space complexity is also O of n because I store the filtered string and its reversed copy.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: That works. Can you think of a way to avoid the extra space?

sections.title: Two Pointer In-Place
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    A["'A man, a plan, a canal: Panama'"] --> B["left=0 points to 'A', right=29 points to 'a'"]
    B --> C["Compare 'a' vs 'a' → match, move inward"]
    C --> D["left skips space and comma, finds 'm'"]
    D --> E["right skips 'm', finds 'a'... continue"]
    E --> F["Pointers meet in the middle"]
    F --> G["All matched → Return true"]
    style A fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style C fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style F fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style G fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: I can use a two-pointer approach. I place one pointer at the start and one at the end. Each pointer skips non-alphanumeric characters. When both point to valid characters, I compare them in lowercase. If they match, I move both pointers inward. If they ever mismatch, I return false.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Walk me through the example with this approach.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: For 'A man, a plan, a canal: Panama', my left pointer starts at 'A' and right pointer at 'a'. Both are alphanumeric. Lowercase 'a' equals 'a', so they match. I move left forward and right backward. Left skips the space and lands on 'm'. Right skips 'm' too. I keep comparing and skipping non-alphanumeric characters. The pointers eventually meet in the middle with all matches, so I return true.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: What about the complexity?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The time complexity is still O of n because each character is visited at most once. But the space complexity is now O of one because I only use two pointer variables and no extra string storage. This is the optimal solution.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Great work. Can you summarize both approaches?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The first approach filters the string and reverses it for comparison. It runs in O of n time and O of n space. The two-pointer approach compares characters from both ends directly on the original string, skipping non-alphanumeric characters. It achieves O of n time and O of one space, making it the optimal solution for this problem.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: The key insight is that palindrome checking naturally fits the two-pointer pattern. By working from both ends inward and skipping irrelevant characters, we avoid building any extra data structure. Well done.
